section_summary: These pages trace efforts from June 1945 through August 1946 to estimate Japanese silk stocks, revive silk production and trade, and decide how imported silk should be priced and distributed. They include proposals from merchants and industry representatives, correspondence with British and Indian officials, and State Department exchanges over the U.S. Commercial Company’s sales methods. The section also contains a separate proposal on Central American abaca plantations and begins a later memorandum assessing Peter Magagna’s criticisms of the Japanese silk program.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing memorandum on Japanese raw silk stocks
subfiles.about: Forwards findings from silk importers on Japanese raw silk stocks.
subfiles.summary: Encloses an inquiry memorandum and offers further help.

subfiles.title: Stocks of Japanese Raw Silk
subfiles.about: Challenges an estimate of 500,000 bales of Japanese raw silk.
subfiles.summary: Importers suggest 50,000–75,000 bales as a speculative figure, citing reduced production, wartime use and bombing.

subfiles.title: Japanese Silk Stocks
subfiles.about: Reports W. A. Spafford’s estimate of Japanese and Italian silk stocks.
subfiles.summary: Spafford envisages 500,000 bales in Japan and a ready postwar American market.

subfiles.title: Cover letter forwarding British inquiry on Japanese silk
subfiles.about: Forwards a British inquiry and asks the State Department to answer.
subfiles.summary: Encloses McDougall’s inquiry and the board’s reply.

subfiles.title: Silk
subfiles.about: Asks about U.S. plans for Japanese raw silk and coordination with British needs.
subfiles.summary: Britain seeks early supplies and considers sending Gaddum to Japan.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of British silk inquiry
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the inquiry and refers it to relevant U.S. agencies.
subfiles.summary: No U.S. supply plans are known to the board.

subfiles.title: Recommendations on Central American abaca projects
subfiles.from: For the Secretary of State, William L. Clayton
subfiles.about: Recommends retaining three abaca plantations in Panama and Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: A State Department subcommittee reviews five United Fruit Company plantations and their contracts, productivity and strategic value. It recommends continuing the Panama and Costa Rica operations, with government support if needed, while inviting the board’s comments.

subfiles.title: Reply on British access to Japanese silk
subfiles.about: Explains pending policy for visits to Japan and allocation of Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Kennedy suggests arranging Gaddum’s visit through British officers on MacArthur’s staff and expects coordination of importing countries’ requirements.

subfiles.title: Mahoney’s commercial history and request to resume Japanese trade
subfiles.about: Seeks a role in renewed textile trade with Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Mahoney describes his prewar silk, rayon, wool and pulp business, including work for Hara & Co. and its manager Shunosuke Yoshimoto. He asks to participate in distributing Japanese raw silk and argues that experienced private merchants should be considered when trade resumes.

subfiles.title: FBI information on Shunosuke Yoshimoto: cover note
subfiles.about: Forwards information from FBI files concerning Yoshimoto.
subfiles.summary: Supplies the requested FBI material.

subfiles.title: FBI file summary on Shunosuke Yoshimoto
subfiles.about: Summarizes Yoshimoto’s affiliations, wartime arrest, internment and repatriation.
subfiles.summary: Records his Hara & Co. position, admitted mercury purchases for Japan, detention in 1942 and later repatriation.

subfiles.title: Mahoney’s account of Shunosuke Yoshimoto
subfiles.about: Recommends Yoshimoto for occupation work on Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Mahoney recounts Yoshimoto’s business career, family, internment and repatriation, and disputes suspicions about his loyalty. He urges State to check Justice Department records and recommend Yoshimoto to occupation officials as a trustworthy silk specialist.

subfiles.title: Ceiling Price for Silk Purchased in Italy or Japan
subfiles.about: Discusses raising the U.S. silk price ceiling to permit purchases abroad.
subfiles.summary: Acheson favors working with U.S. agencies on a higher price, first for Italy and then Japan.

subfiles.title: Restoration of Japanese Silk Trade, earlier copy
subfiles.about: Records talks on Magagna’s Japan mission and U.S. distribution of Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Flood and Magagna seek support for Magagna’s Army mission and favor distribution by experienced private traders. State officials explain the U.S. Commercial Company’s role and express interest in a stable Japanese silk industry.

subfiles.title: Ceiling Price for Silk Purchased in Italy or Japan, copy
subfiles.about: Duplicates the discussion of the silk price ceiling.
subfiles.summary: Acheson proposes finding a workable purchase price with U.S. agencies.

subfiles.title: Restoration of Japanese Silk Trade
subfiles.about: Discusses Magagna’s consultancy and allocation of Japanese silk in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Flood and Magagna seek State’s support for Magagna’s Army assignment in Japan and argue against auction sales or distribution by the U.S. Commercial Company. Officials explain USCC’s broader mandate and suggest that the visitors present their preferred allocation method directly to it. State agrees to emphasize its interest in a continuing Japanese silk industry.

subfiles.title: Telephone note on Mahoney’s trade inquiries
subfiles.about: Records Mahoney’s questions about travel and renewed trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gay says Japanese trade is unlikely to open soon and promises to pass on news.

subfiles.title: Mahoney’s objection to USCC silk marketing
subfiles.about: Objects to USCC’s planned sealed-bid sales and seeks private participation.
subfiles.summary: Mahoney says the proposed sales system would exclude established international merchants. He describes his new associates and again urges use of Yoshimoto’s expertise in Japan.

subfiles.title: Mahoney’s proposal to market Japanese raw silk, recopy
subfiles.about: Offers to market Japanese raw silk for USCC on commission.
subfiles.summary: Mahoney cites financing, storage, staff and prewar experience to propose handling future shipments through his Boston business group.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Magagna’s appointment
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Advises SCAP that Magagna will serve as a silk industry consultant.
subfiles.summary: Requests appropriate assistance for Magagna and promises conversation memoranda by pouch.

subfiles.title: Despatch enclosing conversations on silk
subfiles.about: Forwards two memoranda relating to Magagna’s mission and silk policy.
subfiles.summary: Encloses conversations on the price ceiling and restoration of Japanese silk trade.

subfiles.title: State Department guidance on a permanent silk market
subfiles.about: Urges USCC to develop a lasting U.S. market for Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Asks that sales plans account for long-term demand and be developed with silk industry representatives.

subfiles.title: USCC response on industry consultation
subfiles.about: Responds to State’s request for industry consultation.
subfiles.summary: Schieck says USCC has consulted silk interests and will continue doing so.

subfiles.title: Flood’s revised proposal for silk sales
subfiles.about: Recommends open auctions for Japanese silk under current conditions.
subfiles.summary: Flood reviews the expected route from Japanese producers through the Army and USCC to American buyers. Revising his earlier position, he favors open auctions conducted through the Commodity Exchange’s silk section, with trade participation and sufficient stock on hand, while retaining fixed prices and dealer distribution as his longer-term preference.

subfiles.title: Reply to Flood on Japanese silk
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Flood’s views on selling Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Martin thanks Flood and reiterates his interest in a stable market.

subfiles.title: Offer of Japanese silk fabrics to India
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese silk fabrics potentially available for Indian purchase.
subfiles.summary: Invites discussion of quantities, prices and payment.

subfiles.title: American Silk Council objection to closed bids
subfiles.about: Objects to USCC’s intended closed-bid distribution of Japanese raw silk.
subfiles.summary: Thanks State for its interest but says USCC disregarded industry objections.

subfiles.title: Flood forwards USCC response
subfiles.about: Sends USCC’s reply concerning disposal of Japanese raw silk.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Henderson’s letter for Martin’s information.

subfiles.title: USCC explanation of sealed-bid sales
subfiles.about: Defends sealed bids for initial Japanese silk sales.
subfiles.summary: Henderson argues that shortages favor broad access through sealed bids, with an initial sale near 5,000 bales; USCC will reconsider the method after experience.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to India on Japanese silk piece goods
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese silk piece goods available for India.
subfiles.summary: Requests an early indication of interest in linings, habutae and umbrella cloth.

subfiles.title: Conversation on USCC silk sales and hosiery manufacturers
subfiles.about: Records hosiery industry objections to USCC’s sealed-bid sales.
subfiles.summary: Union and hosiery representatives favor a fixed price with allocation, or open bidding, because they fear sealed bids will disadvantage traditional users. Schieck defends sealed bids as a way to discover prices and obtain revenue for Japanese relief, while saying the method may change after initial sales.

subfiles.title: British arrangements for purchasing Japanese silk
subfiles.about: Confirms discussions of British grading, pricing and shipment arrangements.
subfiles.summary: Britain proposes payment after grading in the U.K. at prices tied to the U.S. market. McDougall also asks about a representative in Japan and confirms that British requirements should pass through the embassy.

subfiles.title: Guidance on foreign purchases of Japanese silk
subfiles.about: Explains tentative international allocations and treatment of foreign buyers in New York.
subfiles.summary: Clayton describes a proposed allocation among prewar purchasers and says foreign buyers generally may purchase in the New York market unless export controls apply. Heavy purchases could require revising allocations.

subfiles.title: Alternate closing page on foreign silk purchases
subfiles.about: States an alternate version of guidance on foreign purchases.
subfiles.summary: Favors a future free silk market in Tokyo and New York.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about silk and rayon shipments to India
subfiles.about: Requests procedures for purchasing Japanese rayon yarn and raw silk for India.
subfiles.summary: Follows up an unanswered telegram and asks for prompt guidance.

subfiles.title: Reply to Matheus-Kerry on Japanese textile purchases
subfiles.about: Explains channels for Indian purchases of Japanese silk and rayon.
subfiles.summary: Directs the firm to the Indian liaison mission in Tokyo and USCC.

subfiles.title: SCAP telegram on market for raw silk
subfiles.about: Recommends sending silk samples to prospective American users.
subfiles.summary: SCAP seeks market guidance, especially for lower grades, odd sizes and 42-denier silk.

subfiles.title: British inquiry on thrown silk and Argentina rumor
subfiles.about: Asks whether U.S. imported Japanese silk yarn is being sold in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Also seeks likely export quantities and prices for thrown silk.

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese silk yarn exports
subfiles.about: Denies the Argentina rumor and describes current Japanese silk imports.
subfiles.summary: Only raw silk stocks are arriving; thrown silk may follow.

subfiles.title: File note on the Flood–Magagna case
subfiles.about: Reports review of Flood’s file and Magagna’s statements.
subfiles.summary: Notes that some of Magagna’s supporting facts were outdated and suggests holding the file.

subfiles.title: Request for summary of Magagna’s demands
subfiles.about: Requests a concise account of what Magagna wants done.
subfiles.summary: Asks staff to omit vague complaints and rhetoric.

subfiles.title: Magagna and the Japanese Silk Program
subfiles.about: Begins an assessment of Magagna’s criticisms of the Japanese silk program.
subfiles.summary: Martin calls accusations against occupation economic staff unsupported and discusses Magagna’s warning about Japanese inflation. The memorandum continues beyond this section.
